DsCP: ICEV Start Stop Idle Energy Saving
Reference: Start-stop systems impose a restart fuel penalty that is commonly approximated as about 7–10 seconds of engine idling. Therefore, net fuel savings are achieved only when the engine-off stop duration exceeds that threshold; for very short stops, the system can provide little benefit or even increase net fuel consumption relative to a conventional vehicle. As a result, the fraction of idle energy actually recovered depends strongly on the driving cycle, especially on total stop time and the number and duration of stop events. In certification cycles with a relatively high stop share, such as the NEDC, start-stop can recover roughly one-half to two-thirds of the theoretical maximum idle-saving potential when restart losses are included. In the WLTC, which has a lower stop share than the NEDC, the potential benefit is smaller. In real-world severe stop-and-go traffic, recovery efficiency can be much higher when stop durations are consistently well above the restart threshold, but any percentage claim should be treated as route- and calibration-dependent rather than universal.
